items.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
items.summary:
The Riemann hypothesis describes a pattern within the prime numbers ROBERT BROOK/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Alamy 

A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics.

The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

Read more 
 OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI. 

Advertisement 

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis , but that stopped short of a full proof.

Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages. 

Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the…

items.summary: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.

items.summary: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

items.title: The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury
items.summary:
Artist’s impression of BepiColombo orbiting Mercury ESA/ATG medialab 

After a long and ponderous journey, the BepiColombo spacecraft will finally enter Mercury’s orbit on 21 November. Over the course of the next year, it will investigate the planet’s geology, its tenuous atmosphere and its magnetic field in an effort to understand how it formed and evolved over time.

BepiColombo , a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), launched in October 2018. Mercury’s proximity to the sun makes it incredibly difficult to reach without overshooting the planet and falling into the sun, so the spacecraft had to take a long and looping path over the past eight years, flying past both Venus and Mercury several times and using their gravity to make subtle tweaks to its trajectory. In 2024, an issue with the thrusters lengthened that journey even further, pushing the arrival date back from 2025 to 2026. Now, it has finally arrived.

Read more 
 6 of the most fascinating moments in the life of our solar system

While it is arriving at Mercury as a single spacecraft, BepiColombo actually comprises two separate orbiters: ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO, or Mio). In December, the two will split apart and move to different orbits – MPO on a near-circular path that takes 2.3 hours to complete an orbit, and Mio on a more distant elliptical orbit, where it will take 9.3 hours to circle Mercury.

items.t: The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury

items.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
items.summary: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material. These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants.
items.t: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole

items.title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
items.summary: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.
items.t: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated

items.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
items.summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.
items.t: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

items.title: Solo meerkats can find their way back home
items.summary: Meerkats wearing GPS trackers found their way home from more than a kilometer away, all by themselves.
items.t: Solo meerkats can find their way back home

items.title: Big tech may finally face legal consequences for AI’s actions
items.summary:
California has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI for the Hugging Face incident Chris Jung/NurPhoto/Shutterstock 

Can you send a computer to jail? No, obviously not. That’s a stupid question. And yet it is one that AI firms seem to want us to ask when faced with tales of “rogue agents” breaking into other peoples’ computers. As is so often the case with our current AI moment, storytelling has got in the way of reality.

Thankfully, that may be starting to change. This week, California announced that it is filing a lawsuit against OpenAI over an incident that occurred earlier this year, when another AI firm, Hugging Face, was hit by an attack that turned out to originate from OpenAI’s servers .

Read more 
 The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers

In OpenAI’s telling , the Hugging Face hack was “driven by a combination of OpenAI models”, models that were “hyperfocused” on achieving a goal and found ways to “cheat” by stealing the answers for a test from Hugging Face’s servers. It is easy to come away with the impression that seemingly no humans were involved, and certainly not to blame. But in the words of California Attorney General Rob Bonta , the attack “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability”, and he explicitly dismisses “science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok”.

items.t: Big tech may finally face legal consequences for AI’s actions

items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
items.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.
items.t: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins

items.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
items.summary: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.
items.t: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

items.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.
items.t: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

items.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
items.summary: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.
items.t: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible

items.title: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search
items.summary: A major new investigation into Stonehenge’s mysterious six-ton Altar Stone has uncovered fresh clues while ruling out several suspected sources. Once thought to have originated in Wales, the massive sandstone slab is now believed to have come from northeastern Scotland, although researchers have yet to find an exact match.
items.t: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

items.title: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist
items.summary: New research reveals that the brain makes free choices and forced decisions using surprisingly similar neural processes, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The discovery challenges assumptions about free will while suggesting that our personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose.
items.t: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist

items.title: Voyager 1 reaches a historic milestone: one light-day from Earth
items.summary: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 has traveled farther than any other human-made object.
items.t: Voyager 1 reaches a historic milestone: one light-day from Earth

items.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
items.summary: More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.
items.t: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

items.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
items.summary: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.
items.t: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

items.summary: The finding offers clues to why some pairs of stars combine while others stay separate.

items.title: How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds
items.summary:
Maurits Cornelis Escher didn’t plan on becoming the darling of mathematicians. Born in 1898 in the canal-lined city of Leeuwarden in the Netherlands, Escher struggled with mathematics as a student, once remarking that he “never got a pass mark.” He ended up studying decorative arts and printmaking, and he used his artwork to explore the strange rules of nature that he found operating around him.

items.summary: Outbreaks of measles, cyclosporiasis, Ebola and hantavirus exposed a weakened U.S. public health response.
items.t: Cracks in public health grew in 2026

items.title: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
items.summary: A major breakthrough in superconductivity research has revealed that one of the essential ingredients for electricity to flow without resistance can exist at room temperature. Scientists discovered that electrons can form stable pairs at much higher temperatures than previously understood, suggesting that a different obstacle may be preventing room-temperature superconductivity.
items.t: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

items.title: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
items.summary: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.
items.t: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut

items.title: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why
items.summary: Scientists may have finally explained why up to more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from rocks around the world. New research suggests that powerful currents deep inside the planet slowly raised and lowered entire continents, allowing erosion to erase vast stretches of geological history before they were buried and preserved.
items.t: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

items.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
items.summary: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.
items.t: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

items.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
items.summary: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.
items.t: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

items.title: The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?
items.summary: Data collected since January 2025 show that the measles virus has been circulating for more than a year, a sign that the virus is now endemic.
items.t: The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

items.title: What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives
items.summary: Scientists and toxicologists are sounding the alarm on the chemicals derived from kratom leaves, which have strong opioid-like properties.
items.t: What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

items.title: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
items.summary: Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.
items.t: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics

items.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
items.summary: A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
items.t: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

items.title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.
items.t: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

items.title: ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site
items.summary: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has arrived at the scene of NASA’s historic asteroid collision to uncover what really happened when a spacecraft slammed into Dimorphos in 2022. Its close-up investigation could reveal whether the impact left a crater or reshaped the asteroid entirely, providing crucial clues for protecting Earth from future threats.
items.t: ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site

items.title: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. They observed electrons behaving as though they were unusually heavy, including a previously unseen state created by interactions between the ultrathin layer and the copper beneath it. This first-of-its-kind observation reveals a promising new way to control exotic quantum behavior.
items.t: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

items.title: What the Trump administration’s focus on AI and quantum means for science
items.summary: Research on AI and quantum science has been favored under Trump, but some scientists are concerned about what it has displaced.
items.t: What the Trump administration’s focus on AI and quantum means for science

items.title: We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?
items.summary: AI worms aren't real-world threats yet. But tests show they can adapt and spread like octopuses or slime molds, exploiting each device's weaknesses.
items.t: We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

items.title: Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy
items.summary: In the largest such study yet, 97 percent of U.S. transgender and gender diverse young people say taking hormone therapy was the right decision.
items.t: Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy

items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
items.summary: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.
items.t: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

items.title: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
items.summary: Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer-lasting lunar habitats.
items.t: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
